Nothing was settled forever, yet they had made one part of the future less dependent on secrecy.
One offered to carry the heavy case, and the other accepted without turning the gesture into a debt.
One torn page could mislead an entire room, so they placed it beside the original seal and checked the date twice.
The archive had survived for years; the challenge was to make its contents useful without turning them into another weapon.
The audience heard two possible explanations, and the pair made clear what observation would distinguish one from the other.
The decision did not solve the mystery, but it prevented a preventable harm, and that mattered to them both.
The evening ended without triumph; it ended with a record that tomorrow’s readers could inspect for themselves.
The older examiner could offer advice, but neither man allowed him to speak on behalf of the surviving candidates.
The promise between them was not that they would always agree, but that disagreement would never be treated as betrayal.
The silence after the discovery was not empty; it gave each person time to understand what might change.
They considered what the record omitted: the names of helpers, the price of delay, and the right to tell another story.
They looked for a second source before moving, since the first account might describe only part of the event.
They refused to break the lock in secret; instead, they gathered two witnesses and recorded the reason for opening it.
They signed below the witnesses, not above them, because the people who bore the cost had to remain visible.
Whatever came next would be judged against the same rules, including those that protected someone they disliked.
A clerk offered a shortcut; they requested the ordinary route in writing, including the name of whoever would approve it.
At sunset they agreed on one limited next step, with a clear point at which either of them could call a halt.
Jiang Mu drew the route in the margin, and Luo Yan added the time beside each turn so another team could check it.
Luo Yan did, more slowly, and left room for a different interpretation.
The old trial had taught people to mistake silence for agreement; both men now insisted that a quiet person could still refuse.
The test of their partnership was whether each could keep his own goal while still protecting the other person’s choice.
There was no shortcut through another person’s suffering; they followed the measured path and kept the lamps lit.
They named the risk before accepting it, and neither treated the other person’s agreement as automatic.
They wrote down exactly what they knew, rather than letting a convincing guess become a fact that no one could challenge.

She learned to remain in the room after the dramatic part was over.
The actual people before Adela did not owe her an easy ending.
The corridors were still narrow, the work still hard, and most questions still open.
The first question was not whether the palace was embarrassed, but whose voice the institution had ignored.
The investigation affected them all, whether or not they had heard Adela’s name.
The note was placed in the public inspection folder, where the time, author, and reason for every correction could be checked.
The promise she could make was narrower: no missing page would be replaced with a convenient guess, and no patient would be turned into a symbol without consent.
The response was imperfect, but it left room for witnesses to approach.
The visitor thanked her for the limits as much as for the information.
Vale's representatives offered an attractive shortcut: a private agreement, a generous payment, and silence from everyone who accepted.
When they found a difference, they recorded it without inventing an excuse.
With the columns separated, neither witness had to be called a liar before the records were examined.
Yet one person had been allowed to choose where to stand and what to say.
